name: Santee Sioux Nation
land_summary: The Santee Sioux Nation is Dakota, descended from bands whose ancestral lands lay in what is now Minnesota. After the U.S.–Dakota War of 1862, Congress voided the Dakota treaties and the United States forced most Dakota people out of the state. In 1863 they were carried by steamboat to Crow Creek in Dakota Territory, where hunger and illness took many lives. In 1866 a presidential order set aside land in northeast Nebraska near the mouth of the Niobrara River, and the Santee Agency moved there. Mission schools followed, including the Santee Normal Training School, founded in 1870. In 1885 families received individual allotments and homesteads, and an executive order opened the remaining reservation land to non-Native settlers; over the following decades much of the allotted land also left Santee hands. In the 1950s the Gavins Point Dam project took land near Santee village on the reservation's eastern edge, and in 2002 Congress approved added compensation for that loss. The nation continues to buy back land within its reservation.

timeline.event: Dakota people forced out of Minnesota after the U.S.–Dakota War of 1862 are taken by steamboat to Crow Creek in Dakota Territory.
A presidential order of February 27 sets aside townships in northeast Nebraska for the Santee, and the Santee Agency is established there, about 13 miles below the mouth of the Niobrara River.
Alfred L. Riggs opens the Santee Normal Training School, which runs for decades on the reservation.
Allotments and homesteads are assigned to Santee families, and a February 9 executive order returns the remaining unallotted land to the public domain; it opens to settlers on May 15.

Congress finds that the Gavins Point Dam project took 593.10 acres of Santee land near Santee village and approves added compensation in the Yankton Sioux Tribe and Santee Sioux Tribe Equitable Compensation Act.

notes: The nation's site (santeesiouxnation.net) refuses automated access, and Wayback copies were blocked, so no nation-published text was used. No reservation acreage is given because sources conflict and none is the nation's: Wikipedia gives 172.99 sq mi, a 2024 ArcGIS story map gives 41,000 acres, and Flatwater Free Press implies about 117,000. Left out for lack of a second independent source: Flatwater's figure that the tribe owns more than 20,000 acres (ICT and the Norfolk Daily News reprinted the same story, so they are not independent); the 1885 allotment acreages (38,908.81 allotted, 32,875.75 homestead, 1,130.70 agency, which appear only in the 1885 Commissioner's report, with Wikipedia as a lead); the Nov 15, 1867 order enlarging the reservation (APP only); the number of Dakota sent to Crow Creek; and the Dec 2025 trust transfer of 5 acres in South Yankton (Nebraska Public Media only). Flatwater calls an '1882 treaty' the reservation's founding. That isn't confirmed anywhere and conflicts with the 1866 order, so it was left out. The 'buy back land' sentence relies on Flatwater alone. It carries no date or number. 'In the 1950s' for Gavins Point rests on the 1955 Corps settlement in the BIA testimony. The statute gives no year of taking. The 1862 war is named but not described.
